verdict: Two rounds covered measurement method well (benchmarks, judges, readability history, reader testing) and the craft literature partly. What is missing is a whole modality: the branch of technical writing where a misread sentence injures someone — aviation/safety procedure writing, controlled language with its field trials, cognitive-accessibility standards — and, with it, every reader who is not a fluent English-reading model. Proven absences from the plugin's own files (grep over /Users/ruliny/Git/agent-skills/plugins/terse/**/*.md): non-native / translation (0 hits), aviation and procedure design (0), center-embedding and Gibson (0), easy-to-read and intellectual disability (0), PEMAT and actionability (0), Stack Overflow / Aghajani / issue-mining as a question source (0), tree testing (0 — round 2 found it and it did not survive into prior-art.md), verbosity bias (0), German/Japanese instruments (0), cognitive load / Mayer / Sweller (0), Göpferich / Langer / reverbalisation (0), information scent (0). The single highest-value gap is provenance of the questions: everything downstream rests on six questions invented by the same party that writes the repair, and nobody has looked at the literature that mines real reader questions or at the standards that dictate who the validators must be. The second is that the headline number's own refutation already sits in prior-art.md:88-91 while the skills still print it bare. Round 3 should be narrow: ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (free on request), Degani & Wiener (already downloaded), Aghajani ICSE 2019, and one reader-language axis. (Tooling note: I installed pypdf into user site-packages to read PDFs; nothing was written into the repo.)

gaps.what: Aviation and safety procedure writing — checklist and procedure design as a writing discipline. Opened: Degani & Wiener, NASA CR-177549, 'Human Factors of Flight-Deck Checklists' (71 pp).
gaps.why: It is the only branch of this field where a wrong reading is counted in wreckage, and it yields rules terse's fixed writing-rules.md does not contain. §6.2.3: a verification step must make the reader state the observed value ('ALTIMETERS 30.10'), never an acknowledgement word ('checked', 'set'), because an acknowledgement can be produced without looking — the ASRS report quoted there is a crew that said 'checked and set' over a wrong airspeed bug. §6.2.4: one name per control across every document (master-lever / start-lever / engine-switch for one thing). §7.1.1: split a long list into chunked task units and separate the chunks graphically. §7.2.1-7.2.2: order steps by system sequence and by the reader's physical path. §8.2.2: place critical items EARLY, where slack exists, rather than next to the moment of time pressure.
gaps.whereToLook: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19910017830/downloads/19910017830.pdf (free, opened, saved at /tmp/degani.pdf; sections cited above at PDF pages 43-45, 51-53, 57). Unopened follow-ons with the same shape: NUREG-0899 and DOE-STD-1029 procedure writers' guides; FAA AC 120-71 SOP guidance.

gaps.what: Controlled language in its real form, plus the two experiments that measured it. ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (Jan 2025): 53 writing rules in 9 sections, ~900 approved words each pinned to one meaning and one part of speech, ~1200 words to avoid.
gaps.why: prior-art.md carries STE only as a 'candidate to test' and records that the standard was never obtained; the field evidence changes what terse's rejection of word limits actually covers. Holmback, Shubert & Spyridakis, CLAW '96 (opened): comprehension study, 130 subjects, four documents (two procedures x SE/non-SE); SE won on the complex procedure and produced nothing on the easy one; non-native speakers benefited most; no time difference, which the authors attribute to the absence of time pressure. Chervak, Drury & Ouellette 1996 (search level, not opened): 175 aircraft maintenance technicians, comprehension error 18% -> 14%, the gain concentrated in the difficult workcards. STE also keeps 20-word (procedural) / 25-word (descriptive) caps while explicitly forbidding shortening by dropping verbs, subjects or articles — a word limit inside a system, not alone.
gaps.whereToLook: Free copy on request at https://www.asd-ste100.org/ (FAQ opened: ~900-word dictionary, free of charge, 'not intended for general-purpose writing'; the FAQ cites no study). Holmback: https://mt-archive.net/90/CLAW-1996-Holmback.pdf (opened, pp. 166-175). Chervak: HFES Proceedings 40(5):303-307 and the FAA field-evaluation report. Prior-art overlap worth recording: danyuchn/asd-ste100-skill references/writing-rules.md is already a Claude Code skill packaging a paraphrase of the rules (opened via gh api).

gaps.what: The reader's language: non-native readers, and documents that will be translated. terse's reader-profile.md has no proficiency axis and no question about translation.
gaps.why: In the only two field studies of a controlled language, that axis carried most of the effect. Holmback pp.170-171 states plainly that English ability beyond native/non-native was never varied and that the population of interest is non-native readers living in non-English-speaking countries; the same paper's translation study (38 translators, three target languages, trained raters, five rated variables) found SE versions scored higher on style match and produced fewer minor omissions. The owner's own worked profile already lists Russian reader phrases ('через codex', 'вторая имплементация') while the rules and the measure assume a fluent English reader.
gaps.whereToLook: /tmp/holmback.pdf pp.167-171 (opened). Then the localisation-facing half of IEC/IEEE 82079-1:2019 and ISO/IEC 26514, neither obtained.

gaps.what: Where the questions come from: mining real reader questions (issues, Stack Overflow, mailing lists, pull requests, site search logs) instead of deriving them from a model-built profile.
gaps.why: Six questions authored by the party that also writes the repair, then reused as the regression test — prior-art.md already names the held-out problem but not the free external source of questions sitting in the repo's own issue tracker. The same literature would test the lie/placement/findability trichotomy against a taxonomy built from 878 real documentation complaints, and the missing fourth category ('the answer is nowhere') is a category in that taxonomy.
gaps.whereToLook: Aghajani et al., 'Software Documentation Issues Unveiled', ICSE 2019, pp. 1199-1210, DOI 10.1109/ICSE.2019.00122 (Crossref metadata opened; the PDF is paywalled at ACM/IEEE and the REVEAL mirror returns 404 — not opened). Follow-up: Aghajani et al., ICSE 2020, 'Software Documentation: The Practitioners' Perspective', pp. 590-601.

gaps.what: Published standards that make reader validation mandatory and name who the validators must be.
gaps.why: terse tests with readers, but its readers are Haiku instances. Every standard that requires validation requires validators drawn from the target group. Opened: Inclusion Europe, 'Information for all: European standards for making information easy to read and understand', p.25 rule 1 — 'Always ask people with intellectual disabilities to test your website.' This is the clause that decides whether the plugin may call its number a reader test, and it is the cheapest external check on the plugin's central claim.
gaps.whereToLook: https://www.inclusion-europe.eu/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/EN_Information_for_all.pdf (opened, 40 pp; the rule is on p.25 of the PDF). IEC/IEEE 82079-1:2019, clause 5 (quality/process) — paid, not opened; the iTeh sample PDF at cdn.standards.iteh.ai exposes the ToC but rendered unreadable through WebFetch. ISO 24495-1's fourth principle is already recorded in prior-art.md.

gaps.what: A second reader instrument that localises the defect: 'optimising reverbalisation with thinking aloud' (Göpferich's Karlsruhe comprehensibility concept).
gaps.why: measure.md forbids asking the reader anything but the answer, and the read log — the concurrent data Schriver calls the reliable kind — is collected and discarded. Reverbalisation keeps the ban on opinion while producing per-detail labels richer than three causes: incomprehensible, hard to understand, misunderstood, or 'demands information the text does not give'. Göpferich's own §3 warns that expert-judgement instruments (which is what terse's judges are) are preparatory and cannot replace target-group testing.
gaps.whereToLook: Göpferich, 'Comprehensibility assessment using the Karlsruhe comprehensibility concept', JoSTrans 11 (2009), 31-51 — free full text at https://jostrans.soap2.ch/issue11/art_goepferich.php (opened; six dimensions in §5: perceptibility, simplicity, structure, correctness, concision, motivation; method described in note 3). Parent model: Langer, Schulz von Thun & Tausch, 'Sich verständlich ausdrücken' (10th ed. 2015) — four dimensions rated by readers on a five-point scale, factor-analytic; book not opened.

gaps.what: Non-English document mechanics. The fixed writing rules are English-shaped and nothing tests whether any of them transfers.
gaps.why: The Japanese technical-writing preset's rules are keyed to characters and particles, not words: sentence <= 100 characters, <= 3 読点 per sentence, kanji run <= 6 characters, no repeated conjunctions, no repeated identical particles, no ら抜き言葉. A Japanese or Russian document cannot be audited by terse's rules at all, and the plugin says nothing about this limit.
gaps.whereToLook: github.com/textlint-ja/textlint-rule-preset-ja-technical-writing, README section ルール一覧 (opened via gh api; rule headings at README lines 104-575). Russian/Belarusian plain language: СТБ 2631-2023 «Ясный язык. Требования к процессу подготовки информации на ясном языке», in force 2024-02-01, and the Russian ГОСТ Р under development by Rosstandart (search level, not opened). German: the Hamburg and Karlsruhe models above; DIN SPEC 33429 for Leichte Sprache.

gaps.what: The sentence-level defect that actually predicts difficulty: dependency distance and center-embedding, not sentence length.
gaps.why: terse rejected hard per-sentence word limits and put nothing measurable in their place; 'counts prompt a review' is the whole rule. Martinez, Mollica & Gibson (Cognition 224:105070, abstract opened via the PubMed API): corpus of ~10 million words across ten genres, two experiments with N=184, and center-embedded clauses inhibited recall MORE than low-frequency jargon, passive voice or non-standard capitalisation — and did so for experienced readers too. That is a measured, checkable replacement rule: hunt long-distance dependencies, not long sentences.
gaps.whereToLook: DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2022.105070; abstract via https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=35257980 (opened). Full text CC BY-NC-ND at MIT DSpace handle 1721.1/148805 (ScienceDirect returned 403 and the DSpace bitstream guess 405 — full text not opened). Companion: Martinez et al. 2023 PNAS on why lawyers write that way.

gaps.what: Instructional-design evidence about writing to one reader profile: cognitive load theory, the expertise reversal effect, and Mayer's coherence-versus-personalization tension.
gaps.why: prior-art.md names Kalyuga once, from an abstract, and nothing in either skill acts on it. terse builds one profile, writes one key from it, and re-measures with readers drawn from the same profile — so text that helps the novice and harms the expert scores as a pure win. The coherence principle (delete) and the personalization principle (add conversational framing) also pull in opposite directions on the same passage, which is exactly the second-pass-cuts-105-words / third-pass-adds-105-back effect the bake-off already observed.
gaps.whereToLook: Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler & Sweller, 'The Expertise Reversal Effect', Educational Psychologist 38(1):23-31, 2003 (tandfonline, paywalled — not opened; claim taken from search summaries and the Springer abstract of Kalyuga 2007). Mayer, 'Multimedia Learning' 3rd ed., coherence and personalization chapters — not opened.

gaps.what: Actionability scored separately from understandability, and a published estimate of how unreliable a prose rubric is between raters.
gaps.why: The judging sheet counts repaired failures and vetoes lies, but never asks whether a reader could act: PEMAT-P splits 24 items into 17 understandability and 7 actionability ('identifies at least one action', 'breaks the action into explicit steps'). And PEMAT's reliability is the closest public number for what two hidden-model judges are doing: mean Cohen's kappa 0.57, range 0.35-0.84, with four trained coders failing to reach agreement after three calibration rounds in one replication.
gaps.whereToLook: AHRQ PEMAT User's Guide, Publication 14-0002-EF — https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications/files/pemat_guide.pdf returned 403 from this host, not opened. Shoemaker, Wolf & Brach, Patient Educ Couns 96(3):395-403, 2014; Lee et al., Health Promot Pract 2022 (the kappa figures; search level, not opened).

gaps.what: Verbosity bias and self-preference in the judges.
gaps.why: bake-off.md makes word count the tiebreak and defaults to Claude agents judging Claude candidates; prior-art #49 covers provider family for the answer key, not the judge's documented preference for longer answers. A plugin named terse whose tiebreak runs with a known length bias would never see the failure.
gaps.whereToLook: Zheng et al. 2023 (MT-Bench / LLM-as-a-Judge), position and verbosity bias sections; Panickssery et al., arXiv 2404.13076, 'LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations' (arXiv fetch timed out — not opened); Dubois et al., length-controlled AlpacaEval, as the mitigation shape. Cheapest local mitigation: score candidates at equal length, or regress length out of the sheet.

gaps.what: A findability instrument that works before the prose exists, and a theory of why readers miss things: tree testing and information scent.
gaps.why: findability is one of three failure causes but is measured only as steps-from-entry, after the text is written. Round 2 found the tree-testing literature and it did not survive into prior-art.md (grep: 0 hits for 'tree test' anywhere in the plugin). Tree testing scores a heading tree with no body text and reports success and directness as two numbers; information foraging explains the miss as weak scent at the link, which is where the repair goes.
gaps.whereToLook: Round 2's own treetest items (Spencer 2003; NN/g success-vs-directness; Optimal Workshop's leaf-nodes-only rule). Pirolli & Card, 'Information Foraging', Psychological Review 106(4), 1999 — not opened.

gaps.what: Structured-authoring standards as a theory of placement: S1000D data modules and information codes, DITA's task/concept/reference typing.
gaps.why: terse's placement cause has no model of what kind of unit a sentence belongs to, and Diataxis was rejected as a mandatory pass without answering the underlying typing question. S1000D encodes the information type into the module's own identifier, which makes 'this sentence is in the wrong kind of unit' a mechanical check rather than a judgement. The specification is free.
gaps.whereToLook: https://s1000d.org/ and users.s1000d.org (Issue 6 download; the site timed out from this host — not opened). OASIS DITA 1.3 specification, topic-type chapters. Note prior-art.md already records the owner's one-liner that confused S1000D with ASD-STE100 — these are two different gaps and both are open.

gaps.what: The plugin's own publication gate, applied to the plugin.
gaps.why: prior-art.md #78 demands that no number reach a README without an n, an interval and a statement of register, and prior-art.md:88-91 already records that the headline is not distinguishable from noise. The skills still print '3/6 to 6/6' bare: measure.md:3-5 and :93-98, revise/SKILL.md:15-16, bake-off.md:7-10. My own recomputation from those six paired items: McNemar exact one-sided p = 0.125 (three discordant pairs, all one way), Fisher two-sided p = 0.18, Wilson 95% CI for 3/6 = [0.19, 0.81] and for 6/6 = [0.61, 1.00].

gaps.what: Run-to-run variance of the reader itself: no arm that re-runs the unchanged document, and no repeated trial per question.
gaps.why: measure.md:25-26 makes one reader per question a rule, for a good reason (freshness), but the consequence is that the instrument has no noise estimate of its own and borrows skillsbench's 30-point floor. Without a repeat arm, 'the score fell' as a refusal condition in revise Step 6 cannot distinguish a damaged rewrite from a different draw.
gaps.whereToLook: measure.md:23-37 and :74-84. Method sources: NIST IR 7804 (already in round 2) for readers per segment; Faulkner 2003, Behavior Research Methods 35(3):379-383, for the spread of problem-discovery across 100 random samples of the same pool (not opened).

convergent: Validate with real members of the target group before publishing, and say who counts as a member — Inclusion Europe 'Information for all' p.25 (opened), ISO 24495-1's fourth principle (already in prior-art.md), IEC/IEEE 82079-1 (not opened), Schriver 1989, Redish, Carroll. Four independent bodies, none connected to each other.

One name per thing, one meaning per word, enforced across the whole document set — ASD-STE100's one-sense dictionary, Degani & Wiener §6.2.4 (nomenclature standardisation across checklists, flight manuals and training manuals), ГОСТ Р 2.105-2019's ban on synonyms for one concept (already in prior-art #63), Vale's consistency check, textlint-rule-terminology.

Make the reader PRODUCE something — an answer, a paraphrase, a reverbalisation, a cloze fill — never rate clarity: Göpferich's reverbalisation protocol, plainlanguage.gov's paraphrase testing, Taylor 1953's cloze, and terse's own 2026-09-10 observation. Four routes to the same rule.

Gains concentrate in hard documents and weak readers; easy documents register nothing — Holmback (SE won on the complex procedure, nothing on the easy one), Chervak (gain only on the difficult workcards), McNamara 1996's reverse cohesion effect, Kalyuga's expertise reversal. This is a moderator, not a detail: it predicts when an audit will measure zero for reasons that have nothing to do with the text.

Measure location separately from comprehension, in the same instrument — Shubert's 1996 two-part items (one part comprehension, one part 'where in the document is this'), tree testing's success-versus-directness pair, terse's steps-from-entry counter. Independently invented three times.
Report a process measure beside the right-answer score — NIST CIF's effectiveness/efficiency pair, Kimble's four-tuple, Carroll's time-to-first-success, Meng 2019's instrumented reads.

Conditions, limits and warnings come before the action, and one instruction per sentence — ASD-STE100's safety rule, plainlanguage.gov, Gopen & Swan's topic position, Degani's challenge-response structure.
Never gate on a metric the writers are also asked to optimise — Bruce, Rubin & Starr 1981; Redish 2000; Pullum 2009; and terse's own 'counts prompt a review, they are not gates'.

Chunk, label the chunk, and keep the unit finishable — Horn's Information Mapping, STE's six-sentence paragraph cap, Degani §7.1.1 (split a 76-item checklist), S1000D data modules, Carroll's short chapters.
singletons: ASD-STE100 Rule 8.1: the semicolon is forbidden outright, while every other standard punctuation mark including the em dash stays. No source outside STE proposes this and STE offers no evidence for it.

Japanese preset: kanji runs capped at 6 characters, at most three 読点 per sentence, no two identical particles in a row. Real defects in Japanese, meaningless outside it — and evidence that a fixed rule list is language-bound.
'Information for all' p.25 rule 3: put the words 'easy-to-read' in the page's meta tag so search engines find it. A 2009 SEO trick shipped inside a comprehension standard.

Degani & Wiener §7.2.2: order steps to follow the reader's physical flow pattern — top of the overhead panel downward, because moving the arms downward is less fatiguing. Correct for a cockpit, inapplicable to a README.
The Hamburg model's fourth dimension, 'zusätzliche Stimulanz' (extra stimulation). It carries the lowest weight of the four in the authors' own analysis and was never validated separately.

Karlsruhe's sixth dimension, 'perceptibility' (layout, fonts, non-verbal elements) — added by one author to one model, and structurally unmeasurable by a model reading raw .md, as the plugin's own formatting section already argues.
PEMAT-P's 'provides a tangible tool' item (a checklist, a planner) — a single instrument's taste about patient leaflets.
Minto's Situation-Complication-Question opening, which withholds the answer and contradicts her own answer-first rule; already flagged in prior-art.md as asserted, not measured.
contradictsUs: Degani & Wiener §8.2.2 contradicts terse's placement remedy. terse says a misplaced true sentence must 'move to the decision it belongs to'. The NTSB-anchored finding is the opposite for critical items: flaps and stabiliser trim were placed at the end of the TAXI checklist precisely to sit near the moment of use, and that tight coupling to a time-pressured segment is named as the defect (Delta 1141). The rule that survives both is: move it to the decision, unless it is critical and the decision is rushed — then move it earlier, into slack.

Holmback pp.171-172 and Chervak both find the effect only on complex documents. A README is an easy document. terse generalises a method from one README, and its own instrument may be structurally unable to register a difference on easy targets — which would show up as a null, not as an error.

terse rejected hard per-sentence word limits; ASD-STE100 keeps 20/25-word caps and pairs them with a one-sense dictionary, one instruction per sentence, a 3-word noun-cluster cap, and an explicit prohibition on shortening by dropping verbs, subjects or articles. terse's rejection was measured against unguided controls in a bake-off, never against a controlled language with a dictionary; the rejection is narrower than the way it is currently stated in writing-rules.md:35-37.

Groeben's counter-position to the Hamburg model: maximum comprehensibility does not maximise retention, and middle difficulty may retain better. If that holds, 'terser' and 'the reader remembers it tomorrow' are different objectives, and the plugin optimises only the first. (Read in a German secondary summary; Groeben 1972/1982 not opened.)

Harding et al., 'AI language models cannot replace human research participants' (AI & Society, 2023/24): LLMs are exemplary text processors by design and therefore will not model human comprehension difficulty — which is precisely the assumption the fresh-reader ruler rests on. Springer redirected to an auth wall; not opened, so treat as a hypothesis with a named source, not a proven result.

Expertise reversal (Kalyuga 2003) plus McNamara's reverse cohesion effect: one profile, one key, one gate cannot see harm done to the other audience. prior-art #26 records both; the skills act on neither.

The headline is not distinguishable from chance, by arithmetic on terse's own six items: McNemar exact one-sided p = 0.125, Fisher two-sided p = 0.18, Wilson 95% CI for 3/6 = [0.19, 0.81]. prior-art.md:88-91 already says so (p = 0.25 two-sided) and adds 'nothing we publish says so' — and the skills still print the bare number in three places.

Göpferich §3: expert-judgement methods are preparatory and cannot replace target-group testing. The bake-off — three writers, two judges, no reader — is an expert-judgement instrument sitting downstream of the only measured one, and bake-off.md already concedes that a bake-off beating a single careful pass is unmeasured.

Every standard that mandates validation mandates the validator: Inclusion Europe requires people with intellectual disabilities to test the text (p.25). terse's validators are Haiku instances drawn from the same family as the writers. Under these standards the plugin's number is a pilot, not a validation.
